overview: This file documents U.S. Consul Edward S. Maney’s observance of American Independence Day in colonial Taiwan in 1935 and 1936. His despatches describe official receptions at the American Consulate in Taihoku attended by senior Japanese colonial and military officials, foreign consuls, American residents, businesspeople, and officials’ wives; they also transmit speeches, an invitation, and translations of local newspaper coverage. The materials emphasize ceremonial expressions of Japanese-American friendship, including reciprocal presidential and imperial toasts and the playing of both national anthems, while also recording practical details such as champagne, shared expenses, formal clothing, extreme summer heat, and ice blocks used to cool the consular residence. A final, apparently displaced State Department memorandum recommends sending a copy of an unspecified item to the Red Cross.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Maney on the 1935 Fourth of July observance
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the official reception and afternoon At Home held at the American Consulate in Taihoku for the Fourth of July in 1935.
subfiles.summary: Maney reports that the morning reception brought together the foreign consular corps, approximately thirty senior Taiwan Government-General officials, and the commander of the Taiwan Army. The ceremony included an address by the Director General, reciprocal toasts to the U.S. president and Japanese emperor, champagne, and recordings of both national anthems. An afternoon At Home attracted about one hundred guests, including approximately thirty Japanese officials’ wives, whose participation followed calls made by Mrs. Maney. Maney also describes using four 250-pound blocks of decorated ice and electric fans to make the consular residence more comfortable in Taiwan’s extreme heat.

subfiles.title: Maney’s response to the Director General’s 1935 congratulatory address
subfiles.to: Director General of Taiwan and assembled guests
subfiles.about: Expresses thanks for the congratulatory address and advocates Japanese-American cooperation, friendship, peace, and social progress.
subfiles.summary: Maney says that the desire for continued cooperation and understanding between Japan and the United States is shared by thoughtful Americans. He argues that nations should concentrate upon relieving poverty and providing economic security. Lasting peace, he concludes, is indispensable to social progress.

subfiles.title: Invitation to the Maneys’ 1935 Independence Day At Home
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney and Mrs. Edward S. Maney
subfiles.about: Invites guests to an afternoon At Home at the American Consulate on Independence Day.
subfiles.summary: The printed invitation announces that the American Consul and Mrs. Edward S. Maney will be At Home at the American Consulate in Taihoku from four to six o’clock on July 4, 1935. It requests an RSVP.

subfiles.title: Newspaper translations on the 1935 Independence Day receptions
subfiles.to: Readers of the Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: Reports the official morning reception and afternoon At Home held by the American consul and his wife on July 4, 1935.
subfiles.summary: The July 4 evening article records the attendance of General Terauchi, Director General Hiratsuka, bureau and court chiefs, the governor and mayor of Taihoku, and foreign consuls at the morning reception. It summarizes Hiratsuka’s praise for traditional Japanese-American friendship and Maney’s response, followed by both national anthems. The July 5 article reports approximately ninety guests at the afternoon At Home, many accompanied by their wives, and names Maney, Mrs. Maney, and Interpreter Matsuo as receiving the guests.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Maney on the 1936 Independence Day observance
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Division of Foreign Service Administration
subfiles.about: Reports the official and foreign-community entertainments held in Taihoku for Independence Day in 1936.
subfiles.summary: Maney transmits his response to the Director General’s July 4 address in accordance with the Consular Regulations. He describes the consular function as a half-hour official reception or champagne lunch attended by the highest-ranking local officials, foreign consuls, and male American residents. The Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo photographed and reported the ceremony. Members of the foreign community were subsequently entertained at the Twatutia Foreign Club, with Maney and two other Americans sharing the cost.

subfiles.title: Maney’s 1936 Independence Day response
subfiles.to: Director General of Taiwan and assembled guests
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese-American friendship as a durable relationship dating from Commodore Perry’s visit to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maney thanks the guests for attending the 160th anniversary observance of American independence. He calls the United States one of Japan’s oldest Western friends and traces the relationship to Commodore Perry’s visit. Although acknowledging occasional differences of opinion, he expresses confidence that goodwill and warm friendship remain the fundamental basis of relations between the two countries and their peoples.

subfiles.title: Newspaper translation on the 1936 reception at the American Consulate
subfiles.to: Readers of the Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: Describes the speeches, translations, toasts, music, and principal participants at the 1936 official reception.
subfiles.summary: The article reports that Director General of Administration Hiratsuka and the bureau chiefs attended the reception at the consular residence in Onari-cho. Hiratsuka’s address was translated into English by Secretary-Translator Koshimura, while Interpreter Matsuo rendered Maney’s response into Japanese. After Commander-in-Chief Yanagawa arrived, Hiratsuka toasted the U.S. president and Maney toasted the Japanese emperor. Recordings of “Kimigayo” and the American national anthem concluded the ceremony shortly after noon.

subfiles.title: State Department note recommending transmission to the Red Cross
subfiles.about: Suggests that the Division of Far Eastern Affairs send a copy of an unspecified document to the Red Cross.
subfiles.summary: This brief Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs note recommends sending a copy to the Red Cross. It is initialed “M.M.H.” and also bears the name James W. McClellan with the date June 13, 1935. A Division of Far Eastern Affairs stamp dated April 25, 1935, appears on the sheet, making its sequence and connection with the Independence Day documents unclear.

interest: The file offers an unusually textured view of routine American consular public diplomacy in Japanese colonial Taiwan, combining formal reporting with speeches, invitations, and Japanese press coverage. Its descriptions reveal the choreography of bilateral ceremony—rank, translation, champagne, reciprocal toasts, anthems, and press photography—as well as the gendered expansion of official sociability through the attendance of Japanese officials’ wives. Details such as Maney’s heavy morning clothes, the four enormous decorated ice blocks, and the sharing of entertainment expenses illuminate the practical and material culture of consular life. The nearly parallel 1935 and 1936 records also allow historians to compare how rhetoric about traditional friendship was maintained during a period of worsening Japanese-American relations, while the anomalously placed Red Cross memorandum illustrates the disorder and residual paperwork sometimes preserved within archival bundles.
